verses.text: Now concerning the collection for the saints, as I commanded the assemblies of Galatia, you do likewise.
On the first day of the week, let each one of you save, as he may prosper, that no collections be made when I come.
When I arrive, I will send whoever you approve with letters to carry your gracious gift to Jerusalem.
If it is appropriate for me to go also, they will go with me.
But I will come to you when I have passed through Macedonia, for I am passing through Macedonia.
But with you it may be that I will stay, or even winter, that you may send me on my journey wherever I go.
For I do not wish to see you now in passing, but I hope to stay a while with you, if the Lord permits.
But I will stay at Ephesus until Pentecost,
for a great and effective door has opened to me, and there are many adversaries.
Now if Timothy comes, see that he is with you without fear, for he does the work of the Lord, as I also do.
Therefore let no one despise him. But set him forward on his journey in peace, that he may come to me; for I expect him with the brothers.
Now concerning Apollos, the brother, I strongly urged him to come to you with the brothers; and it was not at all his desire to come now; but he will come when he has an opportunity.
Watch! Stand firm in the faith! Be courageous! Be strong!
Let all that you do be done in love.
Now I beg you, brothers (you know the house of Stephanas, that it is the first fruits of Achaia, and that they have set themselves to serve the saints),
that you also be in subjection to such, and to everyone who helps in the work and labors.
I rejoice at the coming of Stephanas, Fortunatus, and Achaicus; for that which was lacking on your part, they supplied.
For they refreshed my spirit and yours. Therefore acknowledge those who are like that.
The assemblies of Asia greet you. Aquila and Priscilla greet you much in the Lord, together with the assembly that is in their house.
All the brothers greet you. Greet one another with a holy kiss.
This greeting is by me, Paul, with my own hand.
If any man doesn’t love the Lord Jesus Christ, let him be accursed.  Come, Lord!
The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ be with you.
My love to all of you in Christ Jesus. Amen.

footnotes.content: Paul begins with the collection—money for the poor saints in Jerusalem. Notice how natural it seems to him that churches should care for one another across miles, that abundance in one place helps need in another. This is the body of Christ thinking, not merely tribal loyalty.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "On the first day of the week" — that's Sunday, the Lord's Day. Paul anchors the collection habit to worship itself, suggesting that as we gather to remember the Resurrection, we also remember the poor. Giving becomes part of our rhythm with Him, not a pinch-faced obligation.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Paul will choose carriers *with their approval*, not alone. Even in a matter of money—where control often hides—Paul prefers partnership and trust. He wants the Corinthians to own this gift with their whole selves, not hand it off to a stranger.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Paul leaves room for himself to go too if the Lord wills. He's not yet certain—travel was hard, and he's discerning what the Spirit is saying. This is a man who holds his plans loosely, always open to God's hand redirecting.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He's passing through Macedonia first—visiting the churches there, strengthening them. Paul's travels were never mere logistics; each place mattered. He wanted to see the Macedonian saints before the Corinthians, and that spoke of how he loved them all.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He might even winter with them—stay the full season. You can hear the weariness in that line; an apostle was not spared from cold and hardship. Yet he was willing to be stranded in Corinth if it meant being truly present with them.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He doesn't want a hurried visit—just passing through. Real fatherhood takes time. "If the Lord permits" shows Paul is not pretending to control the future; he's surrendered to the One who does, even in his desire to see them.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Ephesus until Pentecost—that's weeks of waiting and work. Pentecost marks the year's rhythm for a Jewish soul, and Paul was holding his ground in Ephesus until then. Here we see the apostle's calendar woven from both mission and the remembered feasts of his people.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A great door opened—and many adversaries too. Paul noticed both, named both honestly. He wasn't blind to opposition, but he stayed because the harvest field was real. That's faithfulness: not pretending trouble isn't there, but walking through the open door anyway.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Timothy may come to Corinth, and Paul asks that he be welcomed without fear—probably because Timothy was young, perhaps anxious. A leader asks the church to make space for his younger coworker's dignity. How often do we do that for the newer or quieter among us?
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Let no one despise him." A tender line, a grandfather's caution. Paul trusted Timothy but knew the Corinthians' sharp tongues. He sends Timothy forward in peace, already expecting the brothers to receive him. That's what authority looks like: protection for the vulnerable.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Apollos won't come right now, though Paul urged him. No drama here—just respect for a brother's timing. Some churches loved Apollos more than Paul (remember the factions?), yet Paul doesn't resent him or force his hand. That's maturity in ministry.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Watch! Stand firm! Be courageous! Be strong!" After all his travel plans and people talk, Paul sounds the trumpet. The Corinthians faced real wolves—false teachers, idolatry, moral confusion. He calls them to vigilance not from fear, but from love. Faith is active, alert, manly.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Let all that you do be done in love." One sentence that sums it all up. Your firmness, your courage, your watchfulness—none of it matters if love isn't there. Paul keeps returning to this: the greatest thing is love.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Stephanas was the "first fruits of Achaia"—the first household Paul baptized in that province. They had "set themselves to serve the saints," taking on leadership as their own calling. Paul names real people doing real work, honoring them in a way that would be read aloud.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Submit to such people—to those who labor and serve. Authority, for Paul, flows from sweat and sacrifice, not from rank alone. If you want the church to hear you, serve the church first.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Stephanas, Fortunatus, and Achaicus brought Paul news—"supplied what was lacking on your part." They bridged the gap between the apostle and his troubled church. These messengers carried not just words but presence, filling an empty space.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "They refreshed my spirit and yours." How is it Paul's spirit and theirs were refreshed at the same moment? Because when the church is knit together in love, blessing flows both ways. These three didn't just help; they *restored* the whole body.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Aquila and Priscilla, with the church meeting in their house—that couple shows up everywhere, doesn't it? They had a home, and they opened it. That's where the earliest churches often gathered: in ordinary houses, around ordinary tables, with extraordinary Christ at the center.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Greet one another with a holy kiss." This wasn't sentimental—it was the embrace of peace. In a fractious church, Paul calls them back to the gesture itself: meeting face to face, letting the other person matter, sealing fellowship with their bodies as well as their words.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Paul takes the pen. Most of this letter was dictated, but here he signs it himself—"my own hand." In a world where forgeries happened, that signature mattered. But more: it's Paul saying, *I myself stand behind every word here.*
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "If anyone doesn't love the Lord Jesus Christ, let him be accursed." Paul speaks plainly: there is a line. But notice—he sets the condition as love for Jesus, not perfect doctrine or agreement with Paul. The Lord Himself is the test, not tribal loyalty.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Marana tha"—Come, Lord! Readers today hear an echo of that longing. Paul and the early church lived in expectation; they weren't building empires or settling in. They held the work of their hands loosely, knowing the Master could return at any moment. Looking back from our own long road, that urgency feels both distant and needful.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ be with you." After all the instructions, the rebukes, the corrections—grace. Paul ends where the gospel begins and ends. Everything is grace.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "My love to all of you in Christ Jesus." Not "my greetings"—*my love*. Paul knows them. He has argued with them, cared for them, grieved over them. That love is real, not bureaucratic. He signs off with his whole heart.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
